processing: Sun-dried sheng maocha, kept loose or pressed, with no ripe-style fermentation.
harvest_season: Spring is the prized picking, as elsewhere in Yiwu.
appearance_dry: As is typical of Yiwu old-tree tea, long dark-green strands with pale buds.
appearance_liquor: In young tea, a clear, bright gold.
taste_profile: Fragrant and soft like other Yiwu, with a distinctive sweetness, slightly more bitterness than its neighbours, and an aroma that spreads over the tongue and cheeks.

brewing.notes: Full heat suits it. If the bit of extra bitterness dominates, shorten the steep before cutting the temperature.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year, like other sheng, usually as young spring tea from a small maker and sometimes with age. Mansa can mean the village, the old tea mountain or the wider area, and the broad meaning covers much of Yiwu. Ask which one is meant.
description:
Mansa is the old name at the root of Yiwu tea: a village on a high ridge, and one of the historic six tea mountains, sometimes listed jointly with Yiwu. The modern village sits about an hour's walk over a mountain from the Wangong garden of Dingjiazhai.

Its tea is made by ordinary sheng methods. The wider area remains among the best regarded in eastern Xishuangbanna for new-style pu-erh.

Expect a soft, fragrant Yiwu with a slightly bigger bitter edge than most and a sweetness that holds. Brew with hot water and short steeps at first.

The spelling varies, 曼撒 and 曼洒 being the same place, and sometimes the word is used for a whole district. A label that just says Yiwu Mansa does not say much without a village or plot.
history:
Mansa was among the main tea areas of the Qing dynasty and reached its height in the Qianlong era, with accounts of over 300 households and an output reported in tens of thousands of dan. Those figures are traditional and hard to check.

Fires in 1874 and 1887, and later ones, are blamed for its decline, and the trading centre moved to Yiwu.

A local tea king tree is part of its story. It is said to be over 1,000 years old, to have given more than 100 kilograms of fresh leaf in one picking before 1918, and to have lost its main trunk in 1926, with three new shoots growing from the stump. Treat the age as a local claim.
